stops.title: Scout six of twelve pads.
stops.silver: When there are too many states to visit one by one, a table that keeps a separate number for each state cannot learn them all.
stops.do: Twelve pads lie in a row, each hiding a danger number. Walk into a ring with WASD and press F (Interact) to read it. You get 6 reads; each costs a small hit and can be off by 1.
stops.predict: Before you start, choose which 6 pads will tell your team the most about all 12.
stops.saw: Each read lands on its pad and nowhere else, so half the strip is still blank. You just lived Silver's problem at toy size: the budget is smaller than the number of states. In a real game the gap is not 6 against 12 but a handful against more states than atoms.
stops.agent: An agent meets conversations it has never seen in every session, so it cannot keep one stored answer per conversation.

stops.title: Guess which map wins after six calls.
stops.silver: Describe each state by a few features, add them up with weights, and what you learn in one state moves the estimate for every state that shares those features.
stops.do: Your 6 reads fed three maps: EXACT keeps 12 numbers, THIRDS keeps 3, ONE WORD keeps 1. A question floats in front of you. Answer with left click, right click or melee, then read the truth and each map's numbers under the pads.
stops.predict: Commit to the map you think sits closest to the truth on all 12 pads after only 6 reads.
stops.saw: EXACT knows the pads you stepped on and writes 0 on the rest, because a table cannot guess where it has not been. THIRDS writes the average of its third on all four pads, so one read reached four places. Learning that spreads to similar states is called generalisation, and THIRDS usually wins here because of it.
stops.agent: A language model answers a prompt it never saw by its likeness to prompts it did see, which is the same spreading.

stops.title: Predict 60 calls, then press F.
stops.silver: With no teacher to give the true value, the target is the return actually seen, and averaging those returns is unbiased but noisy.
stops.do: The team adds 54 calls, every pad read 4 or 5 times. Answer two questions with the mouse buttons or melee, then press F to bring the calls in and read the table on the right.
stops.predict: Decide which map will be closest after 60 calls, and whether EXACT, which averages each pad's reads, will be exactly right.
stops.saw: With every pad visited, EXACT wins, but its miss is small rather than zero: each pad's number is an average of a few reads that are each off by up to 1. That is lecture 4's Monte Carlo estimate, an average of samples. Look at how little THIRDS and ONE WORD improved between 6 and 60 calls. EXACT is the same method with one group per pad: a table is the special case with one feature per state.

stops.title: Find where THIRDS stays wrong.
stops.silver: An approximator may be unable to represent the true values at all, however much experience it gets.
stops.do: Picture scouting forever, every pad read endlessly. Answer two questions with left click, right click or melee, then read the forever column on the right and the numbers under the pads.
stops.predict: Choose which maps can never get every pad right, and on which pad THIRDS stays most wrong.
stops.saw: With endless reads EXACT reaches 0, THIRDS stops at 1.99 and ONE WORD at 3.39. Most of THIRDS' miss is pad 10, a 9 among 1s and 2s that it calls 3.25, and the same average drags pad 12 up. A coarser description learns faster and has a floor on how right it can get.
stops.agent: When two prompts look alike to a model but need different answers, it gives both the same confident answer, the way THIRDS treats pad 10 like its neighbours.

stops.title: Give one pad its own number.
stops.silver: Good features can make the true value far easier to learn, and choosing them is where the designer's knowledge goes in.
stops.do: Walk into one pad's ring and press F (Interact). That pad gets its own number on top of THIRDS, a map of 4 numbers. Answer one question with the mouse buttons or melee, then read the YOURS row on the right.
stops.predict: Once your pad is picked, commit to how far it will pull THIRDS' forever miss down from 1.99.
stops.saw: Only one pad changes much. Splitting off pad 10 drops the floor from 1.99 to 0.55 with 4 numbers; any other pad leaves it between 1.85 and 1.99, because that pad already fit its group. The number of features mattered less than where they were placed. Choosing the description is most of the work.

stops.title: Read the debrief.
stops.silver: With linear features the best weights come straight from one solve over all the experience, sized by the number of features rather than the number of states.
stops.do: Nothing to press. Read the three lines on the left and your prediction score.
stops.predict: Before you read, say in one sentence what the three maps had in common and what made them differ.
stops.saw: Every map was the same method: the average of the calls in each group, which is exactly the least-squares answer for features that are on in one group and off elsewhere. Only the grouping differed. This was the mildest form of value function approximation, with fixed hand-made groups and plain averages; a neural network learns its own features, and that is where the guarantees thin out.
stops.agent: A value head on a language-model agent reads the whole conversation and learns its features rather than being handed them.
